sections.title: Rubber compound options
sections.chip: 🛑 SBR is what makes cheap step pads perish
sections.live: LIVE → Neoprene, SBR — two of the eight, presented as equals · EPDM, the UV-resistant compound the whole market advertises, is not offered

fields.label: All eight, always — and the market has already named the right one
paragraphs: Margo produces every part in every compound it mixes (client-instructed 2026-09-02). The live selector offers two, understating the offer by six.

🛑 Every accessory brand selling this product advertises the same thing: a UV-resistant rubber step pad. They advertise it because the failure is universal and visible — a step pad goes grey, hard and cracked in two Indian summers, and the customer sees it every time they get in the car.

That failure is ozone and UV attack, and EPDM is the answer. It is the compound the market is describing, and it is not offered on this page. SBR, which is offered, is what the cheap pads are made of — low cost, decent dry abrasion, and poor ozone resistance.
So this page currently offers the compound that causes the market’s known failure, and omits the one that fixes it. Ranking the eight is what turns that around.

fields.label: Selector
rows: UV and ozone resistant — the compound the accessory trade means when it advertises a UV-resistant pad. Holds colour and grip through Indian summers
Best abrasion and tear resistance of the eight — longest tread life, but it perishes faster in direct sun. Specify where the step is sheltered or the pad is replaced on service
The compromise — good weathering, moderate abrasion. Specify where the step also sees oil or fuel spillage
Specify for workshop, plant or fuel-station duty where oil contact is constant
No benefit on a step pad; available if a programme standardises on it

fields.note:
Live set: Neoprene, SBR. Every compound stays selectable; the change is that the page now says which is right and why three are not.
The EPDM-versus-natural-rubber choice is a real one and worth publishing — EPDM lasts longer in sun, natural rubber wears slower under boots. A pad that is replaced at service can be natural rubber; a fit-for-life pad should be EPDM. Ranges are from the locked homepage compound table

paragraphs: 🛑 This part is fitted to a named vehicle, so an industry grid claiming aerospace, marine and oil & gas is evidence the section renders from a site-wide constant rather than the part record.

But the heading is correct, and the fix is not to replace it with a fitment list. Read plainly, “Global Applications” asks two things: where in the world is this sold, and what else does it fit. The section answers both, three cards each, and keeps all six.

The market cards are the commercially useful half. The Scorpio exported from India in volume, and replacement demand follows the parked fleet — so these cards tell a distributor abroad that the part serves their market, and tell Margo where the aftermarket for it actually sits.

sections.title: From compound to certification
sections.chip: Keep · correct process for this part
sections.live: LIVE H2 → From Compound to Certification · six steps · “compression moulding” is right on this page

fields.label: Steps
rows: Material compounding — polymer blending, additive integration and batch QC in our in-house lab. Abrasion resistance and wet grip are set here — a step tread is walked on with grit underfoot.
Mould design & CNC — precision steel tooling manufactured in-house and held as a controlled record. The tread pattern is cut into the tool, so the pattern is a tooling decision, not a finishing one.
Compression moulding — hydraulic press cycles at controlled temperature and pressure. Correct for this part, with transfer moulding where studs or a frame are bonded in
Post-cure & trimming — oven post-cure for dimensional stability, followed by flash trimming. [no change]
Quality inspection — dimensional check, hardness testing and batch sampling before release. Tread depth is the dimension checked, and abrasion is tested per compound.
Export packaging — industrial packing with documentation. ISPM-15 treated pallets where timber packaging is used. Mats are packed flat — a rolled mat holds its curl and will not lie down on the step.
fields.note:
Six steps, six kept — the template’s process is already right on this page. Three steps gain a part-specific detail.
Step 02 is worth expanding here specifically: a buyer who does not know rubber assumes a tread pattern is applied after moulding. It is cut into the tool — which means changing the pattern means changing the tool, and that is a cost conversation worth having before tooling rather than after

notes: The process block must render from the part record even where the default is correct.
Numbered steps are an <ol>.
